subject: Post-call: Dedicated capacity — queueing, routing & concurrency next steps
messages:
From: Tessa Morgan <tessa.morgan@redwood.ai>
To: Priya Shah <priya.shah@quantahhealth.com>, Alex Jensen <alex.jensen@quantahhealth.com>
Cc: Dylan Brooks <dylan.brooks@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 30 Mar 2026 15:12:00 -0700
Subject: Post-call: Dedicated capacity — queueing, routing & concurrency next steps

Hi Priya / Alex — thanks again for the time earlier. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we all have the same view.

Summary of what we heard from your infra & ML teams:
- Primary workload: user-facing clinical summarization + on-demand embeddings for search/rerank.
- Peak pattern: two 20-minute bursts after clinician shift changes (~1:15p/5:15p PT), plus steady baseline of ~35 rps during business hours.
- Latency target: P95 < 220ms for short gen prompts (<= 256 tokens); batch embedding requests acceptable at up to 2s.
- Data constraints: no traffic leaves VPC; we must use Private/Dedicated with customer-managed network (VPN/VPC).

Open architecture questions we discussed to confirm:
1) Auth: you prefer mTLS between your network and our private edge, with API keys for request-level auth.
2) Routing: route clinician requests to low-latency region pool; fallback to warm reserved capacity in another region if capacity saturated.
3) Concurrency & queueing: you'd like hard concurrency caps per-request and a short in-service queue before we spill to a lower-cost model.
4) Structured output / tool-calling: you expect JSON-first responses (schema-validated) and occasional tool-calls to internal search/rerank.

Proposed immediate next steps (action owners & timing):
- Dylan: provide proposed sizing assumptions (GPUs, concurrency per-GPU, token throughput) and a short sketch of the queueing policy by EOD tomorrow. (action: dylan.brooks)
- Priya/Alex: share a representative 24-hour traffic trace (anonymized) and any current P95/P99 latency stats for existing infra.
- Marissa: I’ll prepare a mutual action plan + preliminary estimate to include reserved slots and burst capacity.

Attachments: I’ve attached a first-pass capacity calculator and a simple network diagram for comment (dedicated_capacity_calc.xlsx, network-arch.png).

Can we tentatively schedule a 45m follow-up Thursday to walk the numbers if that works?

Thanks — tessa

--
Tessa Morgan
Director, Solutions | Redwood Inference

Date: Tue, 31 Mar 2026 09:05:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-call: Dedicated capacity — queueing, routing & concurrency next steps

Thanks Tessa — adding technical details on sizing and queue behavior below (quick draft). I’ll flesh into the attached calc shortly.

Assumptions (please confirm with Priya/Alex):
- Model: open-llm-similar (sequence length typically <=512, gen avg 150 tokens).
- GPU perf: ~1,200 tokens/sec per GPU (with quantized runtime on our stack) for beam-1 infer.
- Concurrency per-GPU: target 16 concurrent small-gen requests; for larger batches we prefer queue+batching with 2-4x throughput improvements.

Suggested policy:
1) Front-line limit: request-level concurrency cap at router (configurable per-route). Default: 1,200 concurrent requests overall routed to pool.
2) Per-worker: cap 16 concurrent in-flight streams; extra in-flight requests go to a short in-memory queue per worker (fifo, TTL=800ms) to permit batching.
3) Spill-over: if queue full, route to fallback pool (smaller model/quantized) with higher latency but lower cost.
4) Autoscale triggers: scale-up when 75% GPU utilization sustained for 30s; scale-down when <40% for 90s. Warm-up buffer: keep 2 GPUs hot for fast spin-up during expected bursts.

Embeddings/rerank notes:
- Heavy embedding bursts: prefer batching at ingress (client SDK can buffer up to 200 requests or 10s latency budget). We can provide an SDK helper to collect and submit batches.
- Rerankers: can run on CPU for small candidate sizes; still recommend using a small dedicated GPU pool for larger candidate sets (>500 candidates) to stay under latency SLO.

Auth / routing hooks:
- mTLS for network; then API key / token for per-request identity.
- Router supports per-tenant routing policies (by header or token scope) and route-level tooling enabling structured-output validation before response is returned.

I’ll attach a worked example in the calc: steady-state 35 rps -> 4 GPUs; peak burst 250 rps -> ~12 GPUs (with batching and caching assumptions).

—dylan
From: Priya Shah <priya.shah@quantahhealth.com>

Date: Tue, 31 Mar 2026 09:37:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-call: Dedicated capacity — queueing, routing & concurrency next steps

Thanks Tessa and Dylan — this is helpful. A couple quick clarifications from our infra team:
- The two 20-min bursts are usually ~220-260 rps peak (noted), but those are concentrated into <90s ramp windows. The warm buffer of 2 GPUs may be small for that ramp; can we show a ramp-oriented plan?
- For embedding bursts: we'll likely send 10k embeddings in short windows (these come from batch ETL jobs) and want a cheap batch path (no need for low-latency).
- On structured output: we need a pre-commit validation step — if schema fails, reject and return a structured error that our pipeline can parse.

Attachments: I’ll upload an anonymized 24h trace to the Drive link you shared by EOD.

Can you include a simple ramp simulation (30s/60s/90s ramp) in the calc before Thursday? If so, Thursday 10a PT works for a follow-up.

—Priya

Priya/Alex — I’ve added the tentative calendar invite for Thu 2026-04-01 10:00 PT (accept if that works). We’ll aim to have the calc + ramp sims and a short ops playbook for cutover.

Thanks all — tessa
